newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand details economic rescue plans.
newsitem.headline: Thailand details economic rescue plans.

text.p: Thailand on Tuesday announced sweeping measures to restore investor confidence and revive the sagging economy which include seeking $12-$15 billion in loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and foreign governments.

"The government's first priority is to restore the confidence of the international investors... We realised that the economy is lacking the confidence of investors," said Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya.
"The Thais will be united to solve this problem together," he told a news conference.
The measures included the suspension of 42 of the country's 91 finance firms.
Central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi's announcement on Tuesday of the suspension of the cash-strapped finance firms came on top of 16 companies ordered to stop operations in late June.
Chaiyawat said the newly suspended firms were among those which have borrowed heavily from the central bank this year.
Analysts said the measures were seen as a prerequisite to obtaining IMF facilities or other loans.
The government said it would:
-- maintain at least $25 billion in foreign reserves or an equivalent of the value of 3-1/2 months of imports
-- solve the financial sector crisis by separating healthy financial institutions from troubled ones to boost depositors' confidence
-- cut the current account deficit to five percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 and three percent in 1998 from eight percent in 1996
-- cap annual inflation at 8.0-9.0 percent

-- balance the budget and increase the value added tax to 10 percent effective from August 16, from seven percent now. The government earlier on Tuesday had agreed the hike would be for the 1998 fiscal year starting in October. Prime Minister Chavalit Yonghcaiyudh said separately the government would be willing to cut up to 100 billion baht ($3.23 billion) from the 1997/98 fiscal budget if necessary
-- continue the managed float currency exchange system which was introduced on July 2 to replace the previously tightly controlled system pegged to the U.S. dollar
-- continue tight monetary policy, with interest rates allowed to fall once the financial sector reform measures were implemented
-- not intervene in public utility prices

Once the government implemented the policy, IMF and foreign governments would provide financial facilities through the Bank of Thailand which were expected to be around $12-$15 billion, the government said.
Besides financial assistance, Thailand was also seeking technical assistance from the IMF, said Thanong.

"The details on the amount and terms will be finalised later...Once the package is approved by the IMF, the finance minister and central bank governor will then sign the agreement with IMF," said a government statement.
It did not give a timeframe for when the package would be completed or when the loans might be received.
